sections.heading: What FAA Part 145 adds on top of an NDT certificate
paragraphs: Part 145 is a regulation about organisations. It certifies the repair station, sets out what ratings it holds, and requires a repair station manual and quality control manual that define processes, records and the authority to approve articles for return to service. It does not certify you. This is the distinction candidates get wrong most often.

In practice this means your NDT certification qualifies you for the method, and the repair station's own procedures then determine whether you are on the authorised personnel roster for that method, on that article type, under that rating. Those procedures reference a personnel standard — NAS 410 for aerospace — and add repair-station-specific requirements on training records, continuation training, technique sheets and record retention.

The consequence for a training decision is that Atlanta MRO employers care intensely about the auditability of your qualification record, not just the certificate on the wall. Hours must be evidenced, the practical must have used representative hardware, and the vision test must be current. sections.heading: NAS 410 or SNT-TC-1A: the fork every Atlanta candidate hits

sections.heading: UT thickness and PAUT: what the Ship Channel actually pays for
paragraphs: The volume work in Houston is ultrasonic thickness measurement. Phased array is where the shortage sits. TOFD sits alongside it for girth welds on fabrication and offshore work. Radiography still holds ground on new construction and in fabrication shops, and the choice between the two methods on a given weld is a real engineering decision — we set it out in [RT vs UT for weld inspection](/blog/rt-vs-ut-weld-inspection). title: Phased Array Training: PAUT Level II Hours, Scan Plans and Pay
description: PAUT training beyond conventional UT: focal laws, wedge choice, scan plans, TCG, encoders and S-scan sizing, plus the 80-hour rule and the published pay gap.
h1: What PAUT Level II Training Adds On Top of Conventional Ultrasonic Testing
answer: PAUT training adds the setup skills conventional UT never teaches: focal law calculation, wedge and probe selection, scan plan geometry, encoder calibration, TCG across the aperture, and S-scan interpretation. ASNT specifies 80 hours of Level II phased array instruction on top of UT Level II. Employers expect an unsupervised PAUT Level II to build the scan plan, not just run it.
expansion: The gap that traps most candidates is that PAUT Level II is not a method certification in its own right — it is a technique layered onto ultrasonic testing. Your employer's written practice certifies you in UT; phased array appears as a technique endorsement with its own training hours, its own practical, and its own specific examination. That means the UT Level II prerequisite is not a formality. Beam angle, refraction, DAC construction and thickness-mode calibration all reappear inside the focal law, and a candidate who guessed their way through conventional UT will not survive a sectorial scan where forty-eight angles are alive at once. Before booking a [PAUT Level II course](/paut-level-2-training-course), confirm your written practice actually recognizes the technique endorsement and states the hours — [written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development) is where most programs discover theirs is silent on phased array.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A recommended training hours and the ASNT Education Phased Array Level II course specification (80 hours); scope statements of ASTM E2700, ASTM E2491, ISO 13588 and ISO 18563; ZipRecruiter US wage aggregates for "NDT Level II" (13 February 2026), "Phased Array Ultrasonic Testing" (22 June 2026), "Phased Array Technician" (20 August 2026) and "PAUT Technician" (6 August 2026); Glassdoor US aggregate for ASNT NDT Level III (2026).

facets.q: Do I need UT Level II before starting phased array training?
facets.a: Yes. Phased array is a technique under the ultrasonic method, not a separate method, so your certification reads UT Level II with a phased array endorsement. The focal law is built on the same refraction, velocity and time-of-flight arithmetic taught at conventional UT Level II. Candidates who enter phased array without that foundation can operate the instrument but cannot verify that its depth readings are correct.

facets.q: How many training hours does a PAUT Level II endorsement require?
facets.a: ASNT specifies 80 hours for its Phased Array Level II course, and most US written practices adopt that number for the technique endorsement. It sits on top of the SNT-TC-1A recommendation of 40 hours at UT Level I and 40 hours at UT Level II, giving 160 classroom hours in total. Written practices commonly add three months of documented supervised phased array work before certification is signed.

facets.q: What is the difference between TCG and DAC in phased array?
facets.a: DAC corrects amplitude for attenuation along one fixed angle. A sectorial scan changes angle, metal path and wedge path continuously, so a single curve cannot serve the sweep. Time-corrected gain builds a separate gain-versus-time correction at every angle in the focal law from a reference reflector acquired at several depths. Without it, amplitude falls off at the extremes of the sweep, exactly where the fusion faces are examined.

facets.q: Is an encoder mandatory for phased array weld inspection?
facets.a: Unencoded scanning is legitimate for screening and for locating an indication quickly. Encoded scanning is what produces a re-openable data file with every indication tied to a station along the weld. If the deliverable is a report a third party must audit, or one a repair crew must re-find flaws from months later, the scan needs an encoder and a wheel calibrated against a known distance.

facets.q: How much more does phased array pay than conventional ultrasonic testing?
facets.a: ZipRecruiter put the US average for "Phased Array Ultrasonic Testing" at $87,706 a year on 22 June 2026, against $61,725 for "NDT Level II" on 13 February 2026 — a gap of about 42 percent. The phased array figure sits above the 75th percentile of the general Level II band, which the same source put at $71,500. Certified technique work, not the job title, drives the premium.

facets.q: Can phased array replace radiography on production welds?
facets.a: It does so routinely on carbon steel piping and pressure-boundary welds where the governing code accepts ultrasonic examination in place of radiography for that joint. The operational case is no radiation source, no exclusion zone and no shift shutdown, plus a data file the client can reopen. The technical case rests entirely on a scan plan that proves the coverage a radiograph would have delivered automatically.

sections.heading: Focal laws: the arithmetic that replaces the wedge chart
paragraphs: A focal law is the delay table the instrument applies to each element so the wavefronts from all of them arrive in phase at one point in the part. Change the angle and you change every delay. Change the wedge and you change the entry point, the sound path and the exit point of every element. Conventional UT training hands you a wedge stamped sixty degrees and a chart of skip distances. Phased array training hands you the parameters — element count, pitch, aperture start, angle range and angle step — that generate hundreds of those wedges in software.

The parameters entered wrong most often are wedge velocity, first element height and probe-to-wedge-front distance. All three are printed on the wedge, all three get typed from memory, and all three shift the computed depth of every indication without producing any visible error on screen. A technician who cannot re-derive depth from time-of-flight by hand has no way to catch it. That is the specific reason a UT Level II foundation is a hard prerequisite rather than a recommendation, and why [method training hours by method](/blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method) are structured the way they are.

Good instruction makes you build a focal law from a blank setup on a calibration block, verify it against a known side-drilled hole at three separate depths, and then deliberately corrupt one parameter to see what the resulting error looks like on screen. If a course only walks you through loading a saved setup file supplied by the instructor, you are being taught to operate one particular instrument rather than to apply the technique.

sections.heading: Wedge and probe selection is a coverage decision, not a catalog pick
paragraphs: Wedge choice is a coverage argument. The wedge natural angle sets the center of your usable sweep, and steering more than roughly twenty degrees either side of it collapses sensitivity. Element pitch sets how far you can steer at all, because a coarse pitch throws grating lobes at high angles. Frequency trades penetration against resolution: 5 MHz for general carbon steel weld work, 7.5 or 10 MHz for thin wall and small-diameter tubing, 2.25 MHz where attenuation or coarse grain structure defeats anything higher.

The decision is driven by the joint, not by what happens to be in the case. A 37.5-degree single-V on 25 mm plate demands a different aperture and angle range than a compound bevel on 12 mm pipe with a counterbore. Training that never puts a weld prep drawing in front of you produces technicians who select probes by habit, and habit is how root coverage disappears on the first job that is not a flat plate butt weld with clear access on both sides.

Standards name the technique for exactly this reason. ASTM E2700, Standard Practice for Contact Ultrasonic Testing of Welds Using Phased Arrays, governs manual and semi-automated contact work. ISO 13588 covers the use of automated phased array technology on welds and defines graded testing levels. ASTM E2491 and ISO 18563 cover how the instrument and array themselves are characterized and verified. Knowing which of the four your client's specification invokes is part of the job, and it changes the setup you are permitted to run.

sections.heading: The scan plan is the deliverable employers actually check
paragraphs: The scan plan is the drawing that proves the weld will be covered before anyone squeezes couplant onto the surface. It shows the joint geometry to scale, the probe and wedge sitting on the surface at the index offset you will actually use, and the beam envelope for the lowest and the highest angle in the sweep, first leg and second leg. Every zone of the bevel — root, fill, cap, and the fusion faces on both sides — has to fall inside a beam at some angle in the law.

This is the single element most conventional UT technicians have never produced, and it is the first thing a reviewer looks for. When a phased array report gets rejected by a third party, coverage is almost always the reason: the scan was run, the data looks clean, and nothing in the file demonstrates that the far fusion face was ever insonified. [What makes an NDT report defensible](/report-validation/what-makes-an-ndt-report-defensible) works through the identical failure from the reviewer's side of the table.

Training should have you draw scan plans by hand before it lets you near software that draws them for you. The hand version forces you to reason about index offset, skip distance, and the difference between what the first leg reaches and what the second leg reaches after the beam has spread and lost amplitude. Software will happily render a beautiful, fully covered plan for a geometry that does not exist on the job.

sections.heading: TCG, not DAC: calibrating amplitude across the whole sweep
paragraphs: Conventional UT compensates for attenuation with a DAC curve built on one angle. Phased array cannot do that, because the metal path, the wedge path and the transmission coefficient at the interface all change as the angle sweeps. Time-corrected gain applies a separate gain-versus-time correction at every angle in the law, built from the same reference reflector acquired at several depths. Done properly, a 3 mm side-drilled hole reads the same amplitude at 45 degrees and at 70 degrees, and at 15 mm deep and 40 mm deep.

Building TCG takes real bench time. You place the block, acquire the reference reflector at each depth in turn, and let the instrument solve the curve across the whole aperture. Skipping depths, or building TCG on a block with a different velocity or surface condition than the component, produces a calibration that silently undersizes flaws at the extremes of the sweep — which is precisely where the fusion faces of a bevel are examined and where lack of fusion lives.

Verification matters as much as construction. Re-checking TCG at shift change, after a temperature swing, and after any wedge change is a procedural requirement in most written practices, and it is the evidence auditors ask to see. If your instruction never covers what a failed verification obliges you to do with the data already acquired that shift, it has skipped the part of the technique that protects both you and your employer.

sections.heading: Encoders turn a scan into evidence
paragraphs: An unencoded phased array scan is a live picture. An encoded one is evidence. The encoder wheel reports position along the weld, the instrument indexes each A-scan to that position, and the resulting file can be reopened months later with every indication tied to a station number that a fitter can find with a tape measure, without the technician who acquired it standing on the job to interpret from memory.

Encoder calibration is a two-minute task that gets skipped and then invalidates a full day of data. You roll the wheel a known distance — 500 mm along a straight edge is the common choice — and correct the counts-per-millimetre until the readout matches. Slip on a wet or scaled surface, a wheel dragging against a weld cap, or a magnetic wheel jumping a tack will stretch or compress the C-scan, and the resulting position error is invisible in an otherwise clean image.

Encoded data is what makes phased array competitive with radiography on a shutdown. The argument is not only that there is no source and no exclusion zone; it is that the client receives a re-interrogable data file rather than a film they cannot revisit. A technician who only ever scans unencoded cannot make that argument to a client, and cannot deliver the record that justifies replacing a radiographic technique with an ultrasonic one.

sections.heading: Reading an S-scan: separating a flaw from geometry
paragraphs: A sectorial scan paints every angle in the sweep as a wedge-shaped image with the part geometry overlaid on it. The first skill is separating real reflectors from geometry: the root bead, the counterbore, a backing bar and the far surface all produce strong, repeatable indications that sit exactly where the overlay says the geometry sits. The second skill is recognising which angle a real indication responds best at, because the answer tells you how the reflector is oriented in the weld.

Lack of fusion on a bevel face responds strongly at the angle normal to that face and falls away sharply on either side of it. Porosity responds weakly across the whole sweep and moves erratically as the probe moves. A crack shows tip diffraction — a second, weaker signal above the corner reflector — and that tip is what you measure height from. Slag gives a broad, ragged response with no tip at all. None of those signatures is available on an A-scan alone.

Sizing is where phased array earns its premium and where it is most often done badly. Amplitude sizing carried over from conventional UT overcalls long, low-amplitude planar flaws and undercalls short, well-oriented ones. Tip diffraction and the 6 dB drop applied along the correct axis are the techniques that hold up under review. Practise on flawed samples with known answers — [PAUT Level II practice questions](/blog/paut-level-2-practice-questions) cover the theory, but sizing skill only comes off blocks.

sections.heading: Prerequisites, hours and experience: the real timeline
paragraphs: The route is UT Level I, then UT Level II, then phased array. SNT-TC-1A recommends 40 hours of formal instruction at UT Level I and a further 40 at Level II, with method experience accumulating alongside. ASNT's own Phased Array Level II course is specified at 80 hours, and most US written practices adopt that figure for the technique endorsement. That is 160 classroom hours before anyone can call you a credentialed PAUT Level II, and the hours have to be documented.

Experience is the longer pole. Written practices commonly require three months of supervised phased array work on top of the underlying UT method experience, and that supervision has to be documented by a Level III certified in ultrasonic testing. Companies with no UT Level III on staff cannot sign the certification at all, which is why a training purchase frequently fails to unblock a program that actually has a certification-authority problem rather than a knowledge problem.

Two details cause most rejected certifications. First, the written practice must name phased array explicitly and state its training hours and experience requirement; a document that says only "UT" does not cover the technique endorsement. Second, the specific examination has to be written against the equipment and procedures the technician will actually use — a generic phased array exam bought off the shelf does not survive a client audit. [Written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development) closes both gaps in a single pass.

sections.heading: What a PAUT Level II is expected to do unsupervised
paragraphs: The employer test is not whether you can operate the instrument. It is whether you can walk up to a joint you have never seen, read the weld prep from the drawing or the welding procedure, choose the probe and wedge, build the focal law, produce a scan plan, calibrate TCG and the encoder, acquire the data, and then interpret and report it without a Level III standing behind your shoulder correcting the setup.

That is the entire reason for the pay gap. A conventional UT Level II is paid to execute a technique somebody else designed. A phased array Level II is paid to design the technique on site and defend it to a client inspector who may know the governing standard better than they do. Companies that treat phased array as a button on the machine end up dispatching a Level III to every job, which erases the economics of owning the equipment in the first place.

The functional checklist contractors actually use has four items: build a setup from scratch in under twenty minutes; explain your coverage from the scan plan without notes; produce a report another technician can reproduce from the data file alone; and name the specification clause you are working to. A technician who clears all four moves permanently to the top of the call-out list, and the call-out list is where the money is.

sections.heading: The pay differential, in published numbers
paragraphs: ZipRecruiter's US aggregate for "NDT Level II" stood at $61,725 a year on 13 February 2026, with the 25th percentile at $48,000, the 75th at $71,500 and the 90th at $90,000. Its aggregate for "Phased Array Ultrasonic Testing" stood at $87,706 on 22 June 2026 — about 42 percent above the general Level II figure, and above the 75th percentile of that band entirely. The premium is not a rumour; it is visible in the posting data.

Read title-matched aggregates carefully before quoting them. The same source's "Phased Array Technician" listing averaged $70,578 on 20 August 2026, and its "PAUT Technician" hourly listing averaged $21.53 with a median of $19.71, because those two titles sweep in helper, trainee and assistant postings that are not certified phased array work at all. The distance between $21.53 an hour and $87,706 a year is the distance between a job title and the certification standing behind it.

The differential compounds upward. Glassdoor's US aggregate for ASNT NDT Level III sat at $100,205 a year in 2026, and a UT Level III who is also the phased array authority for a company sits above that, because they own procedure approval as well as interpretation. [NDT Level II salary](/ndt-level-2-salary) and [NDT Level III salary](/ndt-level-3-salary) break the bands out by region and industry. For a scoped cohort on your own instruments and procedures, [request a demo or a quote](/contact).

faq.q: Is PAUT a separate ASNT method or a technique under ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: It is a technique under the ultrasonic method. There is no standalone ASNT phased array method certification; your certificate reads ultrasonic testing, with phased array recorded as a technique endorsement carrying its own training hours, its own practical demonstration and its own specific examination. This matters when you change employers, because the new written practice has to recognise the endorsement before your phased array work is covered.

faq.q: How long does it take to go from UT Level II to working phased array unsupervised?
faq.a: The instruction is 80 hours. The experience most written practices require on top of it is three months of documented supervised phased array work. In practice, technicians who scan daily reach genuine independence — building setups and scan plans without help — around six months in, and technicians who touch the instrument once a month do not reach it at all. Frequency of use matters more than elapsed time.

faq.q: Should I train on the same instrument my employer owns?
faq.a: Train on the technique, verify on the instrument. Focal law construction, TCG, scan plan geometry and sizing transfer across every manufacturer. Menu structure, setup file handling and calibration wizards do not. A course that teaches only one interface leaves you stranded the first time a client supplies different equipment, so the useful sequence is generic technique first, then a short familiarisation on the specific instrument you will carry.

faq.q: Is a practical examination required for a phased array endorsement?
faq.a: Yes, where your employer's written practice follows SNT-TC-1A. The practical requires you to demonstrate the technique on a specimen and report the results, and it is scored alongside a general and a specific written examination. A written practice that omits the practical for phased array is the finding an auditor writes up, which is why the endorsement should be added to the document deliberately rather than assumed under the existing ultrasonic entry.

faq.a: Yes. On-site delivery uses your instruments, your calibration blocks, your written practice and your job geometries as the worked examples, so exam preparation doubles as a program review. That combination also produces the specific examination and the documented hours your written practice needs. Delivery is affordable, accessible and fully customizable to your shift pattern — request a demo or a quote for a scoped cohort.

h1: What the API 653 Exam Actually Tests — and Where NDT Fits In
answer: API 653 certifies you to evaluate aboveground storage tanks, not to run NDT. The exam is 170 questions across a 110-question closed book and a 60-question open book, over 6.5 hours of testing. API charges $1,125 for non-members and $875 for members. Experience runs one to five years depending on your education.

API administers the certification directly with no accredited-provider scheme, so no training company can shorten your eligibility or influence the outcome. Where Atlantis works is the layer beneath the inspector: ASNT method training, Level III procedure approval, and validation of the inspection records a tank inspector signs against.

facets.q: How long is the API 653 exam and how is it split?
facets.a: Roughly seven and a half hours in the chair, six and a half of them actual testing. There are 170 questions: 140 scored and 30 unscored pretest items API is trialling for future exams. The closed-book portion is 110 questions in 2 hours 45 minutes; the open-book portion is 60 questions in 3 hours 45 minutes; a 45-minute lunch break sits between the two. Both are taken in one sitting.

facets.q: What experience do I need to apply for API 653?
facets.a: One year with a bachelor's degree or higher in engineering or technology, two years with a two-year degree or certificate, three years with a high school diploma, and five or more with no formal education. Military technical service substitutes at three and two years respectively. In every tier, at least one year must involve supervising or performing inspection as described in API 653, and all experience must fall inside the last ten years.

facets.q: How much NDT knowledge does the API 653 exam actually test?
facets.a: Narrowly. The body of knowledge names ASME Section V Articles 1, 2, 6 and 7 — general requirements, radiography, liquid penetrant, and magnetic particle limited to yoke and prod techniques — plus Article 23 for SE-797 ultrasonic thickness measurement only. Ultrasonic flaw detection, shear wave weld examination and phased array are not examined. You are tested as the inspector directing and accepting NDT, not as the technician performing it.

facets.q: What does API 653 cost and when are the 2026 exams?
facets.a: API's published initial certification fee is $875 for members and $1,125 for non-members; recertification is $745 and $855. A reschedule costs $350 and a late application $200. The 2026 windows run 13 March to 3 April, 10 to 31 July, and 6 to 27 November, with applications closing 9 January, 8 May and 4 September. Reference documents and travel are additional and usually exceed the exam fee.

facets.q: Is API 653 better to hold than an ASNT Level II certification?
facets.a: They answer different questions. API 653 makes you the person who evaluates a tank's fitness for service and sets its inspection intervals; it is issued to you by API, travels between employers, and renews every three years. An ASNT Level II makes you the person who performs a detection method; it is issued by your employer under their written practice and does not travel. Inspectors holding both are the ones plants call first.

sections.heading: The exam is two exams in one sitting
paragraphs: API 653 runs 170 questions, of which 140 are scored and 30 are unscored pretest items API is trialling for future exams. It splits into a 110-question closed-book portion allowed 2 hours 45 minutes, and a 60-question open-book portion allowed 3 hours 45 minutes, with a 45-minute lunch break between them. That is six and a half hours of actual testing and roughly seven and a half hours in the chair once the tutorial is counted.

The two halves test genuinely different things, and API says so explicitly. The closed book covers knowledge and tasks requiring everyday working knowledge of API 653 and its reference documents. The open book covers detail an inspector is expected to be able to find in the documents but would not normally commit to memory. Candidates who fail usually fail the closed book, because they prepared by learning where things are rather than what they are.

Time pressure is asymmetric across the two portions. The closed book gives you about ninety seconds a question, which is comfortable for recall and tight for the calculations. The open book gives you three minutes forty-five seconds a question, which sounds generous until you are hunting a corrosion-averaging rule across three separate documents. Tabbing and indexing your code books is not a study shortcut — it is the difference between finishing the paper and not.

sections.heading: The reference set you are examined on
paragraphs: The 2026 body of knowledge names eight API publications: RP 571 on damage mechanisms, RP 575 on inspection practices for atmospheric and low-pressure storage tanks, RP 576 on pressure-relieving devices restricted to sections 4.3.2 and 6.7, RP 577 on welding processes, inspection and metallurgy, Standard 650 on welded steel tanks for oil storage, RP 651 on cathodic protection, RP 652 on lining of tank bottoms, and Standard 653 itself. Two ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code sections join them: Section V for nondestructive examination and Section IX for welding qualification.

Editions matter more than page count. API publishes a separate effectivity sheet naming the exact edition, addenda and supplement of every reference that applies to your exam date, and the body of knowledge governing the March, July and November 2026 exams replaced the March 2025 version. Studying a superseded edition is the most expensive mistake in the whole process, because nothing on the exam flags that you are answering correctly from the wrong document. Confirm the current edition before you buy a single publication.

The body of knowledge is equally explicit about exclusions, and reading them prevents a great deal of wasted preparation. Thickness calculations for wind, earthquake and small internal pressures are out. Nozzle calculations for external loads, flange calculations, brazing requirements and venting calculations are out. Welding processes other than SMAW and GMAW are out. Most API 650 annexes are excluded with named exceptions. A third of typical study time gets spent on material the exam will never touch.

sections.heading: How much NDT is on the exam — and which parts
paragraphs: Less than technicians expect, and far narrower. The body of knowledge takes ASME Section V and names only four articles: Article 1 general requirements, Article 2 radiographic examination, Article 6 liquid penetrant including Mandatory Appendix II, and Article 7 magnetic particle restricted to yoke and prod techniques with two paragraphs excluded. Ultrasonics appears through Article 23, and only as SE-797, the standard practice for measuring thickness by manual pulse-echo contact method.

That is the single most useful thing to know about the exam, and almost nobody says it plainly. API 653 does not test you on ultrasonic flaw detection, shear wave weld examination, phased array, or magnetic flux leakage floor scanning. It tests you on ultrasonic thickness measurement, and on applying the surface methods and radiography as an inspector reviewing work somebody else performed. The advanced ultrasonics that actually finds shell and bottom damage sits entirely outside the syllabus.

Which is exactly why the certification and the method credentials are complementary rather than substitutable. A certified tank inspector directs and accepts NDT; an ASNT-certified technician performs it. On a real out-of-service inspection the same shell weld is examined by a Level II working to a procedure written and approved by a [Level III](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services), while the API 653 inspector decides what the results mean for remaining life. [ASNT method training](/training) covers the performing side of that split.

sections.heading: What an API 653 inspector actually does on a tank
paragraphs: The job is evaluation, not examination. You determine corrosion rates from thickness data, average them where the standard permits averaging, calculate minimum required shell thickness course by course, estimate remaining life from those numbers, and set the next internal and external inspection intervals on that basis. You assess settlement against the acceptance criteria, judge whether work is a repair or an alteration, and decide whether a change triggers reconstruction rules and a hydrostatic test.

Interval determination is where the certification earns its keep and where owners most often get it wrong. External and internal intervals are driven by measured corrosion rate, by whether a release prevention barrier and cathodic protection are in place, and by hard ceilings the standard imposes regardless of what the calculation produces. [API 653 inspection intervals explained](/blog/api-653-tank-inspection-intervals-explained) and [atmospheric storage tank external inspection intervals](/blog/atmospheric-storage-tank-external-inspection-intervals) work through both cases with the arithmetic shown.

The written output is the deliverable that gets audited. Inspection records, thickness data sets, calculation sheets and the reasoning linking them have to stand alone years later, when a different inspector opens the file. Most audit findings against tank programs are documentation failures rather than technical ones: the calculation was correct, and nobody can reconstruct how it was reached from the record left behind. The same weakness runs through the NDT reports feeding those calculations.

sections.heading: How API 653 differs from an ASNT method certification
paragraphs: Different issuing model, different scope, different renewal. API 653 is issued by API directly to the individual after a proctored examination, and it travels with you between employers. An ASNT NDT Level II under SNT-TC-1A is issued by your employer against their written practice, and it does not travel — a new employer re-examines and re-certifies you, even in a method you have practised for a decade. That distinction surprises people every single time they change jobs.

Scope differs just as sharply. API 653 covers one asset class across every damage mechanism, code rule and repair decision that applies to it. An ASNT method certification covers one detection technique across every asset class. A UT Level II examines pipe, vessels, tanks and structural steel; an API 653 inspector evaluates tanks using ultrasonic, magnetic particle, penetrant, radiographic, vacuum box and magnetic flux leakage results that other people produced and signed.

Renewal differs too. API 653 recertifies every three years, requiring at least 20 percent of working time spent performing or supervising tank inspection activities, plus 24 hours of continuing professional development, with a 25-question online web quiz every six years under a four-hour limit. ASNT NDT Level III certificates run five years and renew on accumulated points or by re-examination. Employer certifications under SNT-TC-1A follow whatever interval the written practice states.

sections.heading: Cost, windows and the deadline that catches people
paragraphs: API's published initial certification fee for API 653 is $875 for members and $1,125 for non-members. Recertification is $745 for members and $855 for non-members. A reschedule costs $350 and a late application costs $200. Those are examination and administration fees only; publications, review courses and travel sit on top and routinely exceed the exam fee itself. Nothing in the process becomes refundable once the application window has closed.

There are three windows in 2026: 13 March to 3 April, 10 to 31 July, and 6 to 27 November. Applications close roughly two months ahead of each — 9 January, 8 May and 4 September respectively. The deadline is the operative date, not the exam date, and missing one pushes you a full four months down the calendar. [The 2026 API exam schedule](/blog/api-510-570-653-exam-schedule-2026) lays out all three ICP programs side by side so you can plan a sequence.

Budget the documents honestly. The reference set is eight API publications plus two ASME Code sections, and buying them new is a larger line item than the exam fee. Many candidates borrow an employer's controlled copies, which works for study and creates a problem on exam day when the edition on the shelf is not the edition named on the effectivity sheet. Check the sheet against the spines before you begin reading anything.

sections.heading: The realistic route in
paragraphs: Most people who pass came from inspection or NDT work, not from a classroom. The pattern is three to five years as an NDT technician or plant inspector, real exposure to tank turnarounds, and then twelve to eighteen months of deliberate study against the current body of knowledge. Attempting the shortcut — a two-week review course with no tank time behind it — produces candidates who can locate a clause and cannot judge whether the answer it gives them is sensible.

If you are early in a career, the productive move is to accumulate method certifications and tank exposure at the same time. Ultrasonic thickness work on shells and roofs, magnetic particle and penetrant on shell welds and nozzle repairs, and vacuum box testing on bottom seams all count as inspection activity toward the tank-specific year, and all teach you what the standard is actually regulating. That combination is worth more on an application than any single course.

If you already qualify, the sequence is straightforward. Confirm your experience falls inside the ten-year window. Download the current body of knowledge and effectivity sheet. Buy or borrow the correct editions. Work practice calculations until corrosion averaging, minimum thickness and remaining life are automatic. Only then decide whether a review course adds anything you cannot get from the documents themselves and a disciplined schedule.

sections.heading: Where a company needs this and where it needs something else
paragraphs: Owners frequently try to close a tank compliance gap by sending someone to API 653 preparation, when the gap actually sits in the NDT program feeding the inspector. If your thickness data comes from technicians certified under a written practice nobody has reviewed in a decade, a newly certified inspector inherits numbers they cannot defend to an auditor. Separating a credential problem from a program problem before spending money on either is the single highest-return step available.

The other common gap is Level III coverage. An API 653 inspector can accept NDT results but cannot approve NDT procedures or certify technicians — that requires a Level III certified in each method the program uses. Companies without one in-house either cannot certify their own people at all, or are signing certificates with someone who has never examined the procedures. [Level III consulting](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) fills that role without adding permanent headcount.

And if the immediate need is a tank inspection rather than a credential, that is a different purchase entirely. [API 653 tank inspector services](/consulting/api-653-tank-inspector-services) covers the inspection and evaluation work itself, and [report validation](/report-validation) covers independent review of records someone else produced. The distinction is worth being blunt about: Atlantis inspects and evaluates tanks and supports the NDT program behind that work, and does not prepare candidates for the API 653 exam. [Request a quote](/contact) against scope, not against a course.

faq.q: Can I sit the API 653 exam without tank experience?
faq.a: No. Every eligibility tier requires at least one year of experience supervising or performing inspection activities as described in API 653, on top of the general experience the tier demands. A candidate with a bachelor's degree in engineering and one year of pressure vessel work does not qualify; the year has to be tank work. API verifies experience after submission, so an application built on generous interpretation fails at that stage rather than at the exam.

faq.q: Is API 653 a computer-based exam, and can I take it remotely?
faq.a: It is delivered during API's scheduled exam windows, and API states that its non-practical ICP exams are available to take remotely during those regularly scheduled windows. Remote delivery does not change the structure: the same 170 questions, the same closed-book and open-book split, and the same requirement to have the correct editions of the open-book references available in the format the delivery method permits.

faq.q: Which edition of API 653 will be on my exam?
faq.a: Whichever edition the publications effectivity sheet names for your exam date, published separately from the body of knowledge on API's ICP site. The body of knowledge for the March, July and November 2026 exams replaced the March 2025 version, and the effectivity sheet is the document that pins the edition, addenda and supplement of each reference. Check it before buying publications, not after.

faq.q: Do I need an ASNT Level II certification before API 653?
faq.a: No. The two credentials are independent, and API's eligibility routes reference education and inspection experience rather than method certification. Holding a Level II helps in practice, because tank inspection activity performed as a certified technician counts toward the required year and because the exam's NDT content — Section V Articles 1, 2, 6, 7 and SE-797 thickness measurement — is familiar territory to anyone already working under those articles.

faq.q: How often does API 653 have to be renewed?
faq.a: Every three years. Recertification requires that at least 20 percent of your working time was spent performing or supervising tank inspection activities, plus 24 hours of continuing professional development, and API's published recertification fee is $745 for members and $855 for non-members. On top of that cycle there is an online web quiz every six years — 25 questions under a four-hour limit.

faq.q: Our tanks need inspecting and our NDT program needs work. Where do we start?
faq.a: Start by separating the two. An independent look at the written practice, the procedures and the technician certification records tells you whether the data feeding your tank evaluations is defensible, which is a different question from whether you hold enough API 653 certificates. Atlantis covers the inspection work and the NDT program layer beneath it — affordable, accessible and fully customizable. Request a demo or a quote against a defined scope.

title: ASNT Level III Prep San Diego: Basic, Method and Navy Exams

h1: Level III Preparation for San Diego's Ship Repair, Naval Aviation and Defense Manufacturing Base
answer: ASNT NDT Level III requires the Basic exam — 135 questions in four hours — plus one method exam per method: 135 questions in four hours for UT, RT, ET, AE and LT, and 90 questions in two hours for MT, PT, VT, IR and MFL. San Diego demand is driven by ship repair, naval aviation and defense manufacturing, not refining.
expansion: San Diego's Level III demand does not come from refining, because there is no refinery in San Diego County. It comes from a defense industrial base running on written practices tied to NAVSEA and aerospace specifications rather than API. General Dynamics NASSCO — the only full-service shipyard on the US West Coast — plus BAE Systems San Diego Ship Repair and Continental Maritime of San Diego, both Master Ship Repair contractors for the Navy, each need Level III coverage for the methods in their NDT programs. Fleet Readiness Center Southwest at NAS North Island runs depot-level aircraft maintenance, which pulls nondestructive inspection into NAS-410 territory instead. That mix is why a San Diego candidate should choose method exams differently than a Gulf Coast candidate would, and why the [written practice](/compliance/asnt-snt-tc-1a) governing the job you want is worth reading before you book anything.

facets.q: How many exams do I need for ASNT NDT Level III?
facets.a: Two at minimum: the NDT Basic exam, sat once, plus one method exam for every method you want on the certificate. Certifying in ultrasonic and magnetic particle means three exams in total. The Basic is 135 questions in four hours; a UT method exam is another 135 in four hours; an MT method exam is 90 in two. All are computer-based and closed book, at 70 percent to pass.

facets.q: What does the ASNT Basic exam actually cover?
facets.a: Administration of NDT certification programs under SNT-TC-1A and ANSI/ASNT CP-189, plus general principles across acoustic emission, electromagnetic, leak, liquid penetrant, magnetic particle, neutron radiographic, radiographic, thermal/infrared and ultrasonic testing. On top of that it tests materials properties, failure modes, fabrication processes and dimensional metrology. An ultrasonic specialist has to answer neutron radiography and infrared questions cold, which is why the Basic fails experienced technicians.

facets.q: What experience qualifies me to sit ASNT Level III?
facets.a: Three routes. A four-year engineering or physical science degree plus 12 months, counted as 252 days, of NDT experience. Two full academic years of engineering or physical science study plus 24 months, or 504 days. No formal education plus 48 months, or 1,008 days. A day means at least seven hours of work. Experience must be in nondestructive testing, gained under qualified supervision, and documented per method rather than in aggregate.

facets.q: Which employers in San Diego hire NDT Level III?
facets.a: General Dynamics NASSCO, building and repairing ships in the industrial corridor since 1960 and the only full-service shipyard on the US West Coast. BAE Systems San Diego Ship Repair, operating since the mid-1970s on Navy surface warfare ships and commercial vessels. Continental Maritime of San Diego, a Certified Master Ship Repair contractor for the Navy and Military Sealift Command. Fleet Readiness Center Southwest at NAS North Island handles naval aviation depot work.

facets.q: Is there a Level III exam specific to naval shipbuilding?
facets.a: Yes, and it is the most locally relevant thing on this page. ASNT offers a Naval Shipbuilders NDT Level III Specific exam aligned to NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271: 50 questions, two and a half hours, one part, open book, within an employer-based certification system. Candidates preparing only the ASNT Basic and method exams for San Diego shipyard roles discover this one late and unprepared.

facets.q: How long does an ASNT NDT Level III certificate last?
facets.a: Five years. Renewal takes 25 points accumulated across the period, together with continued active employment performing Level III functions in the methods being renewed for at least 36 months — 756 days — of the 60-month term. A candidate who cannot document 25 points recertifies by retaking the method exam for each method held. The Basic is not retaken by a current certificate holder.

sections.heading: Two exams, and the Basic is the one that fails people
paragraphs: ASNT NDT Level III certification requires passing the NDT Basic exam once and one method exam for every method you want recorded on the certificate. The Basic is 135 equally weighted questions in four hours, computer-based and closed book, at 70 percent to pass. It is the exam that ambushes experienced technicians, because almost none of it concerns the method they have spent fifteen years mastering in the field.

The Basic covers administration of NDT certification programs — SNT-TC-1A and ANSI/ASNT CP-189 — plus general principles across acoustic emission, electromagnetic, leak, liquid penetrant, magnetic particle, neutron radiographic, radiographic, thermal/infrared and ultrasonic testing. On top of that it tests materials properties, failure modes, fabrication processes and dimensional metrology. An ultrasonic specialist has to answer thermal and neutron radiography questions from a standing start, with no field experience to draw on.

That breadth is the entire point of the credential. A Level III writes and approves procedures, qualifies and certifies other personnel, and answers to auditors — none of which is method-specific work. Preparation that reads like a UT refresher misses the exam completely. The productive study order is CP-189 and SNT-TC-1A first, then metallurgy and fabrication processes, then a systematic pass across every method you do not personally practise.

sections.heading: What the method exams test
paragraphs: Method exams split by scope. Acoustic emission, electromagnetic, leak, radiographic and ultrasonic testing each run 135 questions in four hours. Thermal/infrared, magnetic flux leakage, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant and visual testing each run 90 questions in two hours. Every one is computer-based and closed book, organised around four topic areas: principles and theory, equipment and materials, techniques and calibration, and interpretation and evaluation of results.

The 90-question methods are not easier per question; they are narrower. A penetrant Level III exam has fewer places for a candidate to hide, which means procedural detail — dwell times, emulsification, developer form, temperature limits — is asked directly and repeatedly. The 135-question methods reward breadth, and candidates lose most of their points in the equipment and calibration blocks rather than in theory. Neither exam gives any credit for field habits that are not written into the standards.

Choose method exams against the written practices you will be signing, not against your résumé. If your employer's program covers ultrasonic, magnetic particle, penetrant and visual testing, a Level III certified only in ultrasonics leaves three methods without an approver, and the company still cannot certify its own technicians in them. That calculation, not personal preference, is what drives most multi-method Level III programs in this market.

sections.heading: Eligibility: what counts, and what a day is
paragraphs: ASNT sets three routes. A four-year college or university degree in engineering or physical science plus at least 12 months — counted as 252 days — of NDT experience. Completion with passing grades of at least two full academic years of engineering or physical science study plus 24 months, or 504 days. No formal education, plus 48 months, or 1,008 days. A day means at least seven hours of work, which is how part-time and split-assignment experience gets converted into countable time.

The experience has to be in nondestructive testing and gained under qualified supervision, in the methods you are certifying in. It is documented per method, not in aggregate across a career. An inspector with twenty years of ultrasonic work and one month of eddy current does not have eddy current experience for Level III purposes, however senior they are on paper. The application asks method by method, and what is submitted is checked.

Level II certification is not itself the entry ticket, but Level II or equivalent experience per method is exactly what the documentation asks you to evidence, and it is the route almost everyone takes. If your Level II certifications were issued under a written practice that is thin on records, assembling that evidence becomes the slow part of the application. [Written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development) fixes the problem on the employer side so the next candidate does not hit it.

sections.heading: The San Diego employer base
paragraphs: General Dynamics NASSCO has designed and built ships in San Diego's industrial corridor since 1960 and is the only full-service shipyard on the US West Coast, producing auxiliary and support ships for the Navy alongside oil tankers and dry cargo carriers for commercial markets, with a substantial repair business supporting the fleet. New construction and repair both generate continuous weld examination, which means ultrasonic, magnetic particle, penetrant, visual and radiographic programs running simultaneously under a single written practice.

BAE Systems San Diego Ship Repair, operating since the mid-1970s, repairs, overhauls and modernises Navy surface warfare ships and commercial vessels at its own yard, at Naval Station San Diego, and at neighbouring yards. Continental Maritime of San Diego is a Certified Master Ship Repair contractor for the Navy and Military Sealift Command, covering shipfitting, welding, pipefitting, machinery repair, marine electrical, sheet metal fabrication and boiler repair. Every one of those trades produces welds that somebody has to examine and somebody has to approve the procedure for.

Fleet Readiness Center Southwest, at the NAS North Island complex, is the largest of the Navy's six main Fleet Readiness Centers, supporting Navy and Marine Corps tactical, logistical and rotary-wing aircraft and their components. Aircraft depot work is a different nondestructive testing world from shipyard work: eddy current on fastener holes and skins, fluorescent penetrant run as a production line, and a personnel qualification regime that looks like NAS-410 rather than SNT-TC-1A.

sections.heading: Why Level III demand exists here, and the exam nobody mentions
paragraphs: Naval work does not run on SNT-TC-1A alone. NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 sets the requirements for nondestructive testing used to determine the presence of surface and internal discontinuities in metals, and contains the minimum requirements necessary to qualify NDT personnel, procedures and equipment. It deliberately does not contain acceptance criteria — those live in the fabrication and repair documents — which forces the Level III to reconcile two document sets rather than work from one.

ASNT offers a Naval Shipbuilders NDT Level III Specific exam aligned to that publication: 50 questions, two and a half hours, delivered as a one-part open-book exam within an employer-based certification system. Candidates preparing for San Diego shipyard roles who study only the ASNT Basic and their method exams routinely find out about this one late in the process. For anyone targeting NASSCO, BAE or a Master Ship Repair contractor, it belongs in the plan from the start.

The practical consequence is that a San Diego Level III usually reconciles three regimes at once: the employer's written practice under SNT-TC-1A, the NAVSEA publication for naval work, and customer or prime-contractor specifications on commercial hulls. Approving a procedure means demonstrating that a technique satisfies all three simultaneously. That is a documentation discipline as much as a technical one, which is why [program audit and gap assessment](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) is a recurring purchase in this market.

sections.heading: The route from Level II
paragraphs: The realistic path is Level II in your primary method, then accumulating documented experience in a second and third method while you study the standards for the Basic. Most successful candidates spend six to twelve months on the Basic alone, because it demands methods they have never operated and administrative content they have only ever encountered from the receiving end as a certificate holder. Nobody passes the Basic on field instinct.

Sequence the exams deliberately rather than by convenience. Take the Basic first if your standards knowledge is weak, because passing it forces the CP-189 and SNT-TC-1A study that makes every subsequent method exam easier to prepare for. Take your strongest method first if your standards knowledge is already solid, because an early pass sustains momentum through a long study period. The certificate itself is not issued until both the Basic and at least one method are behind you.

Between certification and competence sits a gap no exam covers: writing a procedure that survives a customer audit, and qualifying somebody else's technique on equipment you did not choose. Employers in this market read that gap as risk and price it accordingly. [Level III consulting](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) exists because a fresh certificate does not make anyone ready to own a program on day one, and working alongside an established Level III for a cycle is the usual bridge.

sections.heading: Delivery formats that survive a shipyard schedule
paragraphs: Shipyard and depot schedules do not accommodate two consecutive weeks in a classroom. The formats that survive contact with this market are evening or weekend cohorts spread across eight to twelve weeks, on-site delivery inside the customer's own facility built around shift patterns, and self-paced study with scheduled review sessions timed to an exam booking. Any format requiring a technician to vanish from the deckplates during an availability is a format that gets cancelled in week two.

On-site delivery carries a second advantage beyond scheduling. Level III preparation run inside your own facility can use your written practice, your procedures, your equipment and your actual job geometries as the worked examples, which turns exam study into a program review happening at the same time and at no extra cost. Companies certifying several people at once extract far more from [corporate NDT training](/corporate-ndt-training) than from sending individuals to open-enrolment courses out of state.

Whichever format you choose, book the exam before you finish studying. ASNT Basic and method exams are computer-based and delivered at testing centres, seats are finite, and a candidate with no date on the calendar studies indefinitely and sits nothing. [US-based training delivery](/training-usa) covers scheduling around availabilities and shift rotations rather than around a published course calendar built for somebody else's industry.

sections.heading: Choosing methods for this market
paragraphs: In a Gulf Coast refining market, ultrasonic and radiographic testing dominate a Level III's portfolio. In San Diego the weighting shifts noticeably. Ship repair draws heavily on magnetic particle and liquid penetrant for weld and casting examination, on visual testing as a formally certified method rather than an assumed competence, on ultrasonics for thickness and structural welds, and on radiography where joint configuration and access permit it.

Naval aviation shifts the weighting further. Eddy current is a primary method on aircraft structure rather than a specialty, fluorescent penetrant runs as a production line rather than an occasional technique, and the personnel qualification regime is aerospace rather than industrial. A candidate targeting depot work or an aerospace supplier in this county should weight eddy current and penetrant ahead of radiography. Manufacturing suppliers across the county pull in the same direction.

The economical order is: the method your current written practice most urgently needs an approver for, then the method with the highest local demand you can genuinely document experience in, then breadth for its own sake. Certifying in a method where you cannot evidence Level II-equivalent experience wastes an application fee and a study cycle, because ASNT verifies experience method by method rather than accepting a general claim of seniority.

sections.heading: What the certificate obliges you to do, and how it renews
paragraphs: A Level III establishes and approves NDT techniques and procedures, interprets codes, standards and specifications, designates the particular methods and techniques used on a job, qualifies and certifies Level I and Level II personnel, and provides technical direction to them. Where SNT-TC-1A governs, that includes preparing and administering the written practice and the general, specific and practical examinations used to certify everyone below. It is a program ownership role with a technical exam standing in front of it.

ASNT NDT Level III certificates run five years. Renewal takes 25 points accumulated across the period, together with continued active employment performing Level III functions in the methods being renewed for at least 36 months — 756 days — of the 60-month term. A holder who cannot document 25 points recertifies instead by retaking the method examination for each method held; the Basic is not retaken by anyone holding a current Level III certificate.

Pay reflects the responsibility. Glassdoor's US aggregate for ASNT NDT Level III sat at $100,205 a year in 2026, while Salary.com's median for the same title was $88,579 in 2025 — the spread reflects how much of any given role is program ownership versus method execution. [NDT Level III salary](/ndt-level-3-salary) breaks the bands out by region and industry. For a cohort built around your own availabilities and written practice, [request a demo or a quote](/contact).

faq.q: Do I have to hold Level II before applying for Level III?
faq.a: ASNT's published routes are built on education and documented NDT experience rather than on holding a Level II certificate, but the documentation asks for Level II or equivalent experience in each method you are certifying in, which is what almost every candidate satisfies by holding one. The practical answer is that Level II is the normal evidence, and a candidate without it needs an unusually well-documented experience record to substitute.

faq.q: Can I prepare for Level III in San Diego without taking time off work?
faq.a: Yes, and that is the only format that reliably completes here. Evening and weekend cohorts spread over eight to twelve weeks, or on-site delivery inside your own facility timed around shift patterns, both work around ship availabilities and depot production schedules. Two consecutive weeks away from the deckplates does not survive contact with a repair availability, and candidates who commit to that format usually withdraw partway through.

faq.q: Which method should I certify in first?
faq.a: The one your employer's written practice most needs an approver for. If the program covers four methods and only one has Level III coverage, the gap is where your certificate creates immediate value and where the company will fund the attempt. Failing that, pick the method with the strongest local demand you can genuinely document Level II-equivalent experience in, because ASNT verifies experience per method rather than in aggregate.

faq.q: Does Atlantis administer the ASNT exams?
faq.a: No. ASNT administers the Basic and method exams as computer-based tests at brick-and-mortar testing centres, and the Naval Shipbuilders Specific exam within an employer-based certification system. Atlantis prepares candidates for them and supports the program layer underneath — written practices, procedures and technician certification. Preparation is affordable, accessible and fully customizable to your methods and shift pattern; request a demo or a quote.

faq.q: We have no Level III on staff and cannot certify our technicians. What now?
faq.a: That is a certification-authority problem, not a training problem, and sending someone to a course does not solve it for the twelve to eighteen months they need to pass the exams. Interim Level III coverage puts a certified approver over your procedures and examinations immediately while your own candidate works through the Basic and method exams, so certification does not stall and neither does the work.

faq.q: Is the Naval Shipbuilders exam a substitute for the ASNT method exams?
faq.a: No. It is a specific exam covering naval shipbuilding standards aligned to NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, sat within an employer-based certification system, and it sits alongside rather than in place of the Basic and method exams. A San Diego candidate working naval contracts should plan for both tracks, because the employer's written practice and the NAVSEA publication impose separate obligations that a single exam does not discharge.
